segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Some of the most iconic animated characters in film history, such as Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, and Tweety, were created by animators who worked at Warner Bros. Besides entertaining several generations of children and adults, these animated shorts won several Academy Awards and have been incredibly influential on the animation industry in film and TV.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Warner Bros. Animation began when producer Leon Schlesinger (1884-1949), who was distantly related to the Warner Brothers who founded the studio bearing their name, hired two animators, Hugh Harman (1903-1982) and Rudolf Ising (1903-1992), veterans of Walt Disney's cartoon studio in Kansas City. Harman and Ising created the character Bosko, who starred in the studio's first theatrical animated short: Sinkin' in the Bathtub (1930).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Since Walt Disney Productions had launched its Silly Symphony series of cartoon shorts the year before, Schlesinger dubbed his shorts "Looney Tunes," since these shorts initially revolved around music. segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The following year, Warner Bros. launched a second series titled Merrie Melodies, which still revolved around music but featured songs from earlier Warner Bros. films to help sell recordings of those songs. After producing more than 60 cartoons for Warner Bros., the Harman and Ising team split from Schlesinger over salary disputes in 1933, taking their characters with them. The new star of Looney Tunes was initially Buddy—a Bosko look-alike. Buddy was replaced as the series' main star by another Bosko clone named Beans the Cat, who first appeared in 1935 in the Technicolor short I Haven't Got a Hat (1935). However, a much more important character also appeared in that short: Porky Pig. Although Porky was much fatter than in later years, in his first appearance he already had his trademark stutter.

segments.original: One of the main reasons for Porky's success was the influence of animation director Tex Avery (1908-1980), who joined Leon Schlesinger Productions in 1935, and his team of animators, which included Bob Clampett (1913-1984) and Chuck Jones. Under Avery's direction, Porky was redesigned to be "softer" as opposed to fat, and Avery encouraged his animators to develop distinct personalities for the characters that would allow them to stand on their own. He was also a great champion of including rapid-fire gags in every short, a style that would define Warner Bros. cartoons for decades.

Adding to their appeal was voice actor Mel Blanc, "The Man of a Thousand Voices," who gave Porky, Daffy, Elmer Fudd, Bugs, and countless other Warner Bros. cartoon characters their distinctive voices.

segments.original: Avery left Warner Bros. for MGM in 1942, and as the studio's cartoons grew in popularity in the early 1940s, Warner Bros. bought Schlesinger's studio outright and renamed it "Warner Bros. Cartoons, Inc." in 1944. Chuck Jones became the studio's most influential animator, and his cartoons introduced several major characters, including Pepé Le Pew, Marvin the Martian, Wile E. Coyote, and the Road Runner. Other important characters introduced during this period include Tweety (in 1942's A Tale of Two Kitties), Sylvester (in 1945's Life with Feathers), Yosemite Sam (in 1945), and Foghorn Leghorn (in 1946's Walky Talky Hawky). Chuck Jones and other great animators delivered Warner Bros.' greatest classics between the '40s and the '60s, such as What's Opera, Doc? (1957), Duck Amuck (1953), Duck Dodgers in the 24½th Century (1953), One Froggy Evening (1955), and Rabbit of Seville (1950).

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The "Nine Old Men," as Walt Disney himself called them, were the lead animators of Walt Disney Productions during its Golden Age, some of whom later became directors, and they created some of Disney's most famous animated films, from the first feature in history, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, to The Rescuers (1977). Disney delegated more and more tasks to them in the animation department in the early 1950s, as his interests expanded and diversified in scope. All are recognized as legends at Disney and in the world of animation.

tracks.title: The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: The work done by these 9 animators is still used today as a reference in modern animation, and based on the studies they carried out in the '30s and '40s, a template was developed and explained in the book The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation, written by Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, two of the members of the Nine Old Men. The book presents the 12 basic principles of animation: Squash and stretch, Anticipation, Staging, Straight Ahead, Action and Pose to Pose, Follow Through and Overlapping, Action Slow In and Slow Out, Arcs, Secondary Action, Timing, Exaggeration, Solid Drawing and Appeal.

segments.original: Les Clark (1907-1979): There's no doubt that Les Clark's talent earned him a job at the Disney studio, but his nerve also played an important part. As a high school student, Clark worked at a lunch counter where Walt and Roy Disney (1893-1971) often ate. While waiting on them one day, Clark asked Walt for a job; Disney was surprisingly receptive, asking to see some of his work. “So I copied some drawings and showed them to Walt. He said I had a good line and why don't I come to work on Monday,” Clark recalled. Clark graduated that Thursday and went to work for Walt Disney four days later. He assisted animator Ub Iwerks (1901-1971) on the first Mickey Mouse shorts, Plane Crazy (1928) and Steamboat Willie (1928).

segments.original: Ollie Johnston (1912-2008): Joining the Disney Studios as a newcomer in 1935 alongside Marc Davis was Ollie Johnston, who was also hired as an apprentice animator. One of his first projects was a Silly Symphonies short called The Tortoise and the Hare (1935), which won the Oscar for Best Short. Like Kimball, Johnston's lifelong hobby was live steam trains. Starting in 1949, he built a railroad in his backyard, with three 1/12-scale locomotives (later owned by his sons). That railroad was one of the inspirations for Walt Disney to build his own backyard railroad, which later inspired the building of the railroad at Disneyland.

segments.original: Milt Kahl (1909 -1987): Kahl is considered one of the greatest masters in the history of animation, and was the mentor of Richard Williams, author of the book The Animator's Survival Kit and responsible for the animation of Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988). Like Marc Davis, Kahl hoped to find work as a cartoonist. He dropped out of high school to work at the Oakland Post-Enquirer and the San Francisco Bulletin, but after Kahl saw the short Three Little Pigs at a local theater, he decided to try his hand at animation. He was hired by Disney in 1934 as an assistant animator on shorts such as Lonesome Ghosts (1937) and The Ugly Duckling (1939).

segments.original: Ward Kimball (1914 -2002): Kimball, like Kahl, was inspired to become an animator by Disney's short Three Little Pigs. After graduating from the Santa Barbara School of the Arts, he found a job at Disney Studios in 1934 and worked on most of its animated films until his retirement in 1972. Kimball was famous for his sense of humor. He enjoyed perpetuating the rumor that Walt Disney had been frozen: “I always tell people that if anybody was going to be frozen, it would be Walt. Knowing Walt, he was always interested in experiments, always interested in science. He was always interested in 'new' things. He had that kind of personality...”
